curation.lead:
Xenophon Galinas is a Greek-American shipping executive and real estate manager who spent twelve years (1986–1998) running the U.S. operations of the Alexander S. Onassis Foundation, the Liechtenstein-registered entity that controls the Onassis shipping and real estate empire. Trained as a marine engineer (University of Surrey, University of Michigan) with an MBA in finance from NYU, Galinas held concurrent leadership positions across several Onassis subsidiaries: Executive Vice President of Central American Steamship Inc (the Group's non-U.S. flag shipping arm, 1986–1990), President of Olympic Tower Associates (managing the 51-story Olympic Tower condominium at 641–645 Fifth Avenue, 1990–1998), and board member of Williston S.A. (Onassis shipping and real estate). Before joining the Onassis Group, he served as president of Benzopetrol SA in Athens, a family oil, gas, and shipping business that was the exclusive BP/Greece transport partner, and oversaw its sale to BP interests in 1986.

Galinas enters the Epstein investigative record through a single documented transaction. In March 1996, he negotiated with both Jeffrey Epstein and the State Department's Office of Foreign Missions to take over the lease at 34 East 69th Street, a former Iranian deputy consul general residence that Epstein had leased since February 1992 at $15,000 per month and then abandoned in January 1996. Galinas and OFM reached a letter agreement on April 12, 1996, for a five-year lease at $16,000–$18,000 per month, with Galinas separately agreeing to pay Epstein $100,000 for improvements to the property. The agreement was expressly subject to Epstein's right of first refusal. On April 16, Epstein exercised that right — not to return to the property, but to block Galinas and instead sublet to criminal defense attorney Ivan Fisher at $20,000 per month, capturing a $5,000 monthly profit on the government lease. OFM denied written consent for the Fisher sublet, but Epstein proceeded anyway, triggering the federal ejectment action United States v. Epstein (96 CIV 8307, SDNY) before Judge Denny Chin (EFTA01325008).

Exhaustive searches across the DOJ Volume 11 corpus (331,000 pages), DugganUSA, LMSBAND, the Unified database, email archives, financial records, FARA, LDA, Deutsche Bank DS10 transactions, and OpenSanctions returned zero results for Galinas outside the judicial opinion. He does not appear in any Epstein contact list, email, flight log, or financial record. The available evidence indicates that Galinas was an unwitting counterparty in a commercial real estate transaction — a senior shipping executive seeking prestige office space on the Upper East Side who happened to negotiate for a property that Epstein was exploiting for profit. After leaving the Onassis Group in 1998, Galinas moved into shipping investment banking (ASA Holdings/Pacific Millennium, Morgan Joseph TriArtisan, Rodman & Renshaw), co-founded Manhattan Group Partners and Manhattan Maritime Enterprises Inc (a $114 million blank-check SPAC headquartered at 645 Fifth Avenue), served on the board of FreeSeas Inc (an Athens-based dry bulk shipper, 2012–2017), and currently operates as CEO of Manhattan Maritime Capital.
open_questions: Was Galinas specifically recruited through Onassis Foundation or Greek shipping network channels to take the 34 East 69th Street lease, or did he find the property through ordinary commercial real estate channels? The answer would clarify whether Epstein's OFM property was marketed within a specific social circuit.

Is Vassilios (Bill) M. Livanos, Galinas's co-founder at Manhattan Maritime Enterprises, related to the George Livanos who appears on Epstein guest lists and whose private island Coronis was referenced in Peggy Siegal's 2017 email to Epstein? A confirmed family connection would establish a second-degree link between Galinas's business network and Epstein's social network.

What happened to the $100,000 improvement payment that Galinas had agreed to make to Epstein? The letter agreement with OFM was conditioned on Epstein's right of first refusal, which Epstein exercised. Did Galinas make any partial payment before the deal collapsed, or was the arrangement entirely prospective?

Did the Onassis Foundation or Olympic Tower Associates have any other documented interactions with Epstein-linked entities beyond the 34 East 69th Street transaction? Olympic Tower at 645 Fifth Avenue appears over 1,000 times in the Epstein corpus, but review suggests these are incidental venue references rather than substantive connections.
curation.system_role: Galinas is an example of a peripheral figure drawn into the Epstein record through a routine commercial transaction rather than any network participation. His significance lies in what the failed lease negotiation reveals about Epstein's operational methods in the mid-1990s: using government-custodied property as a profit vehicle, exercising contractual rights strategically to block legitimate deals, and misrepresenting State Department authorization to subsequent tenants. The Galinas episode also establishes that Epstein's 34 East 69th Street property was known in elite NYC real estate circles connected to the Onassis Foundation and Greek shipping networks.

sections.title: Twelve Years Running the Onassis Empire in America
sections.content:
Galinas joined the Onassis Group in 1986 after selling the family shipping and petroleum business, Benzopetrol SA of Athens, to BP interests. The Alexander S. Onassis Foundation — registered in Liechtenstein at Heiligkreuz 6, Vaduz (LEI 529900ZJX6MJVD7ORF75), with a parallel public benefit foundation (LEI 529900BNVA9LZUGD2U08) created in December 1975 and a U.S. nonprofit arm (EIN 13-4037172) based in New York — entrusted him with progressively greater authority over its American operations. From 1986 to 1990, he served as Executive Vice President of Central American Steamship Inc, the Onassis subsidiary managing non-U.S. flag shipping. In 1990, he was elevated to President of Olympic Tower Associates, the entity responsible for the 51-story Olympic Tower condominium at 641–645 Fifth Avenue, built by Aristotle Onassis in 1976. He simultaneously held a board seat on Williston S.A., overseeing the Group's combined shipping and real estate interests.

ACRIS records show Olympic Tower Associates engaged in 37 NYC property transactions during the period of Galinas's presidency — 17 as grantor and 20 as grantee — at addresses including 645 Fifth Avenue Suite 301 and 888 Seventh Avenue. The New York Secretary of State confirms Olympic Tower Associates LLC (DOS ID 2585540) as a domestic LLC filed December 20, 2000, in New York County, distinct from the later Olympic Tower Manager LLC (DOS 4310987, a Delaware foreign LLC from 2012) and the unrelated Olympic Towers Associates LP in Erie County. The Foundation's corporate structure spans multiple jurisdictions: Liechtenstein for the parent foundations, BVI for Onassis Management SA (now lapsed, via ATU General Trust in Ruggell), and New York for the U.S. charitable and real estate operations. Galinas's role placed him at the center of this cross-border apparatus, managing its most visible American asset from a Fifth Avenue address that would appear over 1,000 times in the Epstein document corpus — though overwhelmingly in incidental references to Olympic Tower as a gala and event venue, not in any connection to Galinas personally.

sections.title: The 34 East 69th Street Transaction
sections.content:
The single documented intersection between Galinas and Jeffrey Epstein occurred in the spring of 1996 over a lease at 34 East 69th Street, a former Iranian diplomatic residence held as blocked property by the State Department's Office of Foreign Missions. Epstein had leased the building since February 1992 at $15,000 per month, with an extension through January 1997 that included a right of first refusal. He abandoned the premises in January 1996 but continued paying rent, retaining his contractual position.

In March 1996, Epstein began negotiating simultaneously with Galinas and with Ivan Fisher, a prominent criminal defense attorney. Galinas's proposed arrangement included a $100,000 payment to Epstein for improvements made during Epstein's tenancy. But Galinas also contacted OFM directly, and on April 12, 1996, he and OFM executed a letter agreement for a new five-year lease beginning February 1, 1997, at $16,000 per month with annual increases to $18,000. The agreement was expressly conditioned on Epstein's right of first refusal. OFM informed Galinas that it would not consent to Epstein subletting beyond January 1997.

Four days later, on April 16, 1996, Epstein exercised his right of first refusal — not to occupy the property himself, but to block the Galinas–OFM deal. He then sublet to Fisher at $20,000 per month on May 7, 1996, despite OFM's express written denial of sublease consent on April 26. Epstein told Fisher the State Department had orally approved the arrangement, a claim that OFM representative Richard Massey would later deny under oath. The scheme netted Epstein $5,000 per month ($60,000 per year) in arbitrage between his government lease rate and Fisher's sublease payment. OFM terminated Epstein's lease on August 23, 1996, triggering the federal ejectment action United States v. Epstein (96 CIV 8307, SDNY). Epstein's transaction counsel for the OFM negotiations was Jeffrey Schantz; his litigation counsel was Wachtel & Masyr LLP (Steven J. Cohen, with Jesse Masyr as partner). Judge Denny Chin granted summary judgment and ordered ejectment of all occupants on April 1, 1998 (EFTA01325008).

sections.title: From Foundation Management to Shipping Finance
sections.content:
After departing the Onassis Group in 1998, Galinas pivoted from institutional asset management to shipping investment banking. He served as President of ASA Holdings, later renamed Pacific Millennium NA, managing international bulk shipping investments from 1998 to 2004. In March 2004, he co-founded Manhattan Group Partners LLC with Vassilios (Bill) M. Livanos, a fellow Greek-American shipping executive with over 25 years in U.S. maritime management. The two operated from 645 Fifth Avenue — the same Olympic Tower address where Galinas had spent twelve years with the Onassis Foundation.

In July 2005, Galinas and Livanos filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC for Manhattan Maritime Enterprises Inc (CIK 1331764), a Delaware-incorporated blank-check company targeting $114 million for shipping acquisitions. Galinas served as Chairman, CEO, and Secretary; Livanos as President. The founders loaned $220,000 to the company and paid $7,500 per month to Manhattan Group Partners for office space at 645 Fifth Avenue. Ladenburg Thalmann served as underwriter, with trust funds held at Smith Barney/Citigroup. The IPO appears never to have been completed — no subsequent SEC filings exist for the entity. Galinas then moved through roles at Morgan Joseph TriArtisan (Managing Director, Head of Shipping, 2009–2011) and Rodman & Renshaw (Managing Director, 2011–2012) before serving as an independent director of FreeSeas Inc (CIK 1325159), an Athens-based dry bulk shipping company listed on NASDAQ, from 2012 until his resignation in February 2017. SEC records show 55 filings mentioning Galinas across FreeSeas proxy statements and annual reports. The SEC revoked FreeSeas's registration in August 2022. Galinas currently operates as CEO of Manhattan Maritime Capital.

The Livanos connection raises a peripheral investigative question. The Epstein document corpus contains three references to the Livanos shipping family: EFTA02389898 records a July 2017 email from social broker Peggy Siegal to Epstein about dining on the private island Coronis, owned by Greek shipping tycoon George Livanos and his wife Lita; EFTA02421758 lists George Livanos on an Epstein contact or guest list compiled by Lesley Groff. Whether Vassilios (Bill) Livanos is related to George Livanos of the storied Livanos shipping dynasty has not been confirmed, but both Galinas and the Livanos family operated within the same NYC Greek shipping social and business circle that peripherally intersected with Epstein's social network.

sections.title: The Significance of Comprehensive Negative Results
sections.content:
The investigative value of the Galinas dossier lies substantially in what is not there. Exhaustive searches across every available Epstein document corpus — the DOJ Volume 11 (331,000 pages), DugganUSA (204,000 records), LMSBAND (60,000 records, 851,000 entities), the Unified database (70,000 records), and the Investigations database — returned zero results for Galinas outside the single judicial opinion (EFTA01325008) in the DugganUSA corpus. He does not appear in any Epstein email, communication, contact list, flight log, or investigative report. Negative results also extend across regulatory databases: zero FARA registrations, zero LDA lobbying filings, zero UCC liens, zero FAA aircraft registrations, zero OpenSanctions entries, zero Deutsche Bank DS10 transactions for Galinas or any Onassis entity, zero UK Companies House presence, and no LittleSis relationship mapping.

FEC records do show eight political donations between 1994 and 1997 totaling a net $2,000 — all Republican (Bob Dole, Alfonse D'Amato, and Greek-American congressman Mike Bilirakis of Florida's 9th district), with employer listed as Olympic Tower Associates and Onassis Group at zip code 10022. This modest Republican donor profile, anchored in the Greek diaspora political network, is consistent with a shipping executive operating primarily through Greek and Liechtenstein corporate structures rather than American regulatory frameworks. Galinas was not a named party in either federal case arising from 34 East 69th Street — United States v. Epstein (96 CIV 8307) or Epstein v. Fisher (1:97-cv-01489) — despite his lease negotiations being central to the factual record establishing Epstein's motive for blocking the deal. His role was that of an unwitting third party whose legitimate commercial activity exposed the mechanism of Epstein's property manipulation scheme.
